How structurally consequential is a person's typical merged PR — not how many PRs they merge, and not how many lines or files each one touches.

The intuition

If you change a file that only you ever touch, the blast radius of getting it wrong is small — you find out, you fix it, nobody else was depending on it. If you change a file that a dozen other engineers also regularly touch, you're operating in shared, load-bearing territory: more people are depending on that code being right, and more people would be affected if it weren't. Shipped Scope tries to measure the second thing — how many other engineers' work intersects with yours — using nothing but "who touched which files, when," which is the one signal GitHub data can give cleanly.

The formula

for every file in the 90-day window:
    file_weight(file, this_PR) = sqrt(
        count of OTHER engineers (not this PR's author)
        who also touched `file` somewhere in the window
    )

PR_reach = mean(file_weight) across all files the PR touches

Engineer_reach = mean(PR_reach) across all of the engineer's
                 merged, non-mechanical PRs

Shipped Scope = percentile_rank(Engineer_reach) across all engineers

Why sqrt()

Without damping, a file touched by 40 other people would count for literally 40x a file touched by 1 other person — a single very "hot" shared file (a core schema, a widely-imported utility) would dominate the whole score for anyone unlucky or lucky enough to touch it. Square-rooting compresses that: going from 1 co-toucher to 4 only doubles the weight, not quadruples it. It still rewards touching shared territory — it just stops one hotspot file from swamping everything else.

Why average across files, not sum

Summing the per-file weights within a PR would mean a 20-file PR automatically scores higher than a 1-file PR, structural consequence held equal — the PR would win on file count alone, which is exactly the kind of size-proxy this metric exists to avoid. Averaging measures the PR's typical file, regardless of how many files it happens to touch.

Why average across PRs, not sum

This is the more important of the two averages. Summing an engineer's per-PR contributions across all their merged PRs would mean whoever simply merges the most PRs wins, even with the per-file averaging fix in place — someone with 400 PRs of modest reach can out-accumulate someone with 20 PRs of very high reach. Averaging measures the typical consequence of this person's work, which is what "impact per PR" is actually supposed to mean, and is what makes it possible for someone with very few but very consequential PRs to rank highly (see the worked example below).

This is a proxy for structural reach, not business impact. Touching code many engineers depend on is a real, defensible signal — but GitHub data cannot tell you whether that code shipped a feature customers loved or fixed a bug nobody noticed. Shipped Scope answers "how load-bearing is this person's typical change," not "how much revenue did it generate."

Worked example

Two toy engineers, three files in the window, to make the arithmetic concrete.

FileTouched byOther engineerssqrt(weight)
billing/invoice.pyalice, ben, cho, dan31.73
billing/currency.pyalice, ben11.00
billing/README.mdalice only00.00

Alice ships one PR that touches all three files above:

PR reachmean(1.73, 1.00, 0.00) = 0.91
Engineer reach (1 PR)0.91

Ben ships five small, low-traffic PRs elsewhere in the codebase that nobody else happens to touch that quarter:

PR reach (each of 5 PRs)0.00 (no co-touching engineers)
Engineer reach (5 PRs)0.00

Alice ends up ranked above Ben on this component despite merging one-fifth as many PRs — because her single PR sat in genuinely shared, consequential territory, and averaging (rather than summing) means Ben's extra volume in low-traffic code doesn't out-accumulate that. This is the exact case an earlier, buggy version of this metric got backwards: it summed rather than averaged, so Ben's volume alone would have won.

What's excluded going in

  • Mechanical PRs (lockfile-only diffs, dependency bumps) don't contribute a file-touch record to the shared map at all — otherwise a lockfile, which nearly every PR in a monorepo touches at merge time in some workflows, would look like the most "consequential" file in the repo for reasons that have nothing to do with engineering judgment.
  • Bot-authored PRs are excluded the same way, for the same reason.

← Methodology / Leverage on Others

35% of the Impact Score

Leverage on Others

How much has this person helped teammates ship, measured by substantive code review — the clearest force-multiplier signal GitHub data can show.

The intuition

Shipping your own code is direct impact. Reviewing someone else's code well — catching a bug, pushing back on an approach, asking the question that saves a production incident — is leveraged impact: it improves work you didn't personally write, and it scales with how many different people you help, not just how much code you personally produce. This component tries to isolate that specific signal from the much noisier stream of "review" activity GitHub actually contains.

What counts as a review, here

Not every review submission counts. A review only qualifies if:

  • its state is APPROVED or CHANGES_REQUESTED — an actual verdict, not a bare comment thread; and
  • its body is longer than 20 characters — enough to rule out a bare "LGTM 👍" or "+1" as a substantive contribution.

Reviews from automated tools — CodeRabbit, Greptile, PostHog's own internal review bot (stamphog), and similar — are excluded entirely, on both sides of the calculation (as a reviewer, and as someone whose PR was reviewed).

The formula

substantive_reviews = count of qualifying reviews this engineer gave
distinct_authors    = count of different people whose PRs they reviewed

Leverage_raw = substantive_reviews × log(1 + distinct_authors)

Leverage on Others = percentile_rank(Leverage_raw) across all engineers

Why multiply by log(1 + distinct authors)

Ten substantive reviews spread across eight different teammates represents broader, more valuable help to the team than ten substantive reviews given to the same one person over and over — the second pattern looks more like a close mentor/mentee pair than org-wide leverage. The log1p term rewards breadth without letting it run away: going from reviewing 1 person to 8 people matters a lot; going from 8 to 16 matters less per person, which log-damping captures naturally.

Worked example

Two engineers, each with exactly 10 substantive reviews in the window:

EngineerReviewsDistinct authors reviewedlog(1+n)Leverage_raw
Concentrated — reviews mostly one teammate1010.696.9
Broad — reviews spread across the team1082.1921.9

Same review count, but "Broad" scores roughly 3x higher — the formula is measuring how many different people were helped, not just how many review actions were taken.

What this deliberately doesn't include: review speed. An earlier version of this metric added a small bonus for fast review turnaround, measured as time from PR creation to this reviewer's first review. That interval includes time before the reviewer was ever actually asked to look at the PR, so it wasn't measuring responsiveness — it was measuring something closer to "how quickly did anyone happen to look at this," which isn't attributable to a specific reviewer. Rather than ship a plausible-looking number built on a shaky timestamp, it was removed. Leverage on Others is currently pure count-and-breadth, nothing time-based.

← Methodology / Domain Stewardship

20% of the Impact Score

Domain Stewardship

Which parts of the codebase does this person's activity concentrate in strongly enough that they're one of the one or two most active people there right now.

The intuition

Some engineers are broad generalists; others become the person a team leans on for a specific area — auth, billing, the experimentation engine, whatever it is. Neither is better, but "who would you go ask about X" is a real, distinct kind of impact from either shipping code or reviewing it, and it's visible in the data as concentration of activity within a scope.

A naming correction. This component was originally called "Ownership / Trust Routing," which overclaimed what the underlying data shows. Authored-plus-reviewed activity in a scope is evidence that someone is currently active and concentrated there — it is not evidence that a team lead or process actively routed work to them, which would require data this dashboard doesn't have (assignment history, on-call rosters, team charters). "Domain Stewardship" describes what's actually measurable: activity concentration, not routing.

How a PR's scope is determined

PostHog's PR titles mostly follow a conventional-commit style — feat(scope): …, fix(scope): … — so the scope is parsed directly out of the title when present:

feat(billing): add proration for mid-cycle plan changes
      ^^^^^^^
      scope = "billing"

When a title has no scope prefix, the dominant top-level directory among the PR's changed files is used instead (e.g. most files under frontend/scenes/experiments/ → scope frontend). This fallback fires on a small minority of PRs — the current rate is shown in the dashboard's freshness line — and is disclosed rather than silently treated as clean signal.

The formula

for each scope (e.g. "billing", "flags", "ai-research"):
    rank engineers by (PRs authored in this scope) + (substantive reviews given in this scope)
    #1 in that ranking earns  +2 stewardship credit
    #2 in that ranking earns  +1 stewardship credit
    everyone else earns 0 for this scope

Engineer's raw stewardship = sum of credits across every scope they appear in

Domain Stewardship = percentile_rank(raw stewardship) across all engineers

Why top-2-per-scope, not a continuous share

A continuous measure (e.g. "what % of this scope's total activity is yours") would reward someone who does a little bit of everything roughly as much as someone who's clearly the go-to person for one specific area. Restricting credit to the top two per scope makes the signal binary and legible: either you're one of the one or two people most active in an area right now, or you aren't. It also means a single prolific generalist can't quietly accumulate credit across every scope just by touching all of them lightly — they have to actually be top-2 in each one.

Worked example

Two toy scopes, four engineers:

ScopeEngineerAuthored + reviewedCredit
billingdana14+2
eli9+1
fay30
flagsdana20
eli11+2
EngineerTotal raw stewardship
dana2 (billing only)
eli1 + 2 = 3 (top-2 in billing, top-1 in flags)
fay0

Eli ranks highest here — not because of raw volume, but because he's a top performer in two different scopes rather than the single top performer in just one.

What's excluded going in

Mechanical PRs don't count toward any scope's activity, for the same reason they're excluded from Shipped Scope — a wave of dependency-bump PRs in a scope shouldn't manufacture stewardship credit for whoever happened to merge them.

input.content:
← Methodology / Percentile Ranking

Cross-cutting, applies to all three components

Why percentile ranks, not raw scores

Each component (Shipped Scope, Leverage, Domain Stewardship) produces a raw number first — a co-touch weight, a review count, a credit total. Before it's combined into the Impact Score, that raw number is converted to a 0–100 percentile rank. This page explains why.

The problem with the raw numbers directly

The three raw values live on completely different, incompatible scales — a Leverage raw score might be "22," a Shipped Scope raw score might be "0.9," and a Stewardship raw score might be "3." There's no honest way to average those together with fixed weights (45% / 35% / 20%) without first putting them on the same footing.

Why not min-max scaling

The obvious fix — rescale each component so the lowest value maps to 0 and the highest maps to 100 — breaks badly in a dataset this size, because a single extreme outlier compresses everyone else into a narrow band near the bottom:

Raw valuesMin-max scaled
1, 2, 3, 4, 400, 2.6, 5.1, 7.7, 100

Four engineers who differ meaningfully from each other (1 vs. 4 is a 4x difference) all get flattened into single-digit scores because one person happens to be an extreme outlier. In a 90-day window across 200+ engineers on a very active repo, an extreme outlier is close to guaranteed — min-max would make the scores misleading by construction.

What percentile ranking does instead

percentile_rank(value) = (average rank position among all engineers, 0-indexed)
                          / (total engineers - 1) × 100

Every engineer's percentile depends only on how many people they outrank, not on the absolute gap between values. The same raw values from above, percentile-ranked instead:

Raw valuesPercentile ranks
1, 2, 3, 4, 400, 25, 50, 75, 100

The five engineers are now evenly spread out, which is the honest picture: relative to their peer group, each one is meaningfully ahead of the last, regardless of how far out in front the single outlier happens to be. Ties are handled by averaging the tied ranks, so two engineers with identical raw values always get identical percentiles.

Why a raw value of exactly zero always shows as zero

Percentile rank on its own has one sharp edge: since it only measures relative position, even someone with zero substantive reviews given will land above rank 0 if anyone in the dataset has a negative or otherwise-lower value — or in practice here, will simply land at whatever percentile corresponds to "tied for last," which is not automatically 0 when many engineers share that same zero value. Left alone, that can show someone with literally no qualifying activity in a component at a nonzero-looking percentile, which reads as partial credit for something that didn't happen. The ranking function special-cases this: any engineer whose raw value is exactly zero is pinned to a 0 percentile in that component, full stop, regardless of how many other engineers also happen to be at zero.

Net effect: a component score of 0 always means "no qualifying activity," a score of 100 always means "highest in the dataset," and everything in between reflects standing relative to peers rather than a raw magnitude that different components can't otherwise be compared on.

Review data is capped and may hide human reviews behind bot reviews. `reviews(first: 10)` in fetch_prs.py has no `totalCount`/`pageInfo` captured, so there's no way to tell if a PR's real review list got truncated. 1,737 PRs (11.5%) show exactly 10 fetched reviews (the cap), meaning automated reviews (coderabbitai, greptile, stamphog, etc.) can consume those 10 slots before human reviews even get fetched, silently hiding real human review activity. Add `totalCount` and `pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }` to the reviews field, and paginate to fetch all reviews for PRs where `hasNextPage` is true (or at minimum, do a full re-fetch for the current top-20 candidates so the eventual top-5 is trustworthy — your call on scope vs. GraphQL budget, but the top-5 must be based on complete review data).

4. Review turnaround measures the wrong interval. scripts/score.py (~line 167-182) computes turnaround as `review.submittedAt - pr.createdAt`, which includes time before the reviewer was ever requested — not a real "how fast did they respond once asked" signal. We do not have review-request timestamps in the current fetch (no `reviewRequests` field, timestamps aren't retroactively available via GraphQL for already-resolved requests in a way that's cheap to add reliably). Simplest correct fix: drop the 20% speed modifier from Leverage on Others entirely and make that component pure `count * log1p(distinct_authors)` unless you find a cheap reliable way to get real request-to-first-review timing — don't fake it.

CREDIBILITY FIXES (apply all):

- Rename "Ownership / Trust Routing" to "Domain Stewardship" everywhere (index.html labels/legend/methodology copy, and score.py's internal naming/comments if it aids clarity) — authored+reviewed activity per scope shows stewardship of an area, not that work was actively routed to that person by others, which the old name overclaimed.
- Percentile (rank_normalize) currently gives nonzero percentiles to engineers with zero raw contribution in a component (observed floors: 0.7 shipped, 24.2 leverage, 21.8 ownership) because it's a pure rank/(n-1)*100 regardless of the underlying raw value. Fix rank_normalize (or wrap it) so that a raw value of exactly 0 always maps to a displayed 0, regardless of rank.
- The "How this works" methodology copy in index.html claims mechanical-PR exclusion covers "lockfile-only diffs, dependency bumps, bulk codemods" but `is_mechanical()` in score.py only actually detects dependency-bump titles and lockfile-only file changes — no bulk-codemod detection exists. Either implement a real bulk-codemod heuristic (e.g. very high file count + very low per-file diff / generated-file path patterns) or remove "bulk codemods" from the copy so it doesn't overclaim.
- The stored `why_overrides` text for richardsolomou (in data/scores.json, currently only manually patched, not generated by any script) claims "the highest per-PR structural reach in the top five," but ReeceJones's Shipped Scope percentile (96.7) is actually higher than richardsolomou's (93.0). Change the wording to "among the highest."
- rafaeelaudibert's why_overrides text says "50 substantive reviews across 65 collaborators," but the 65 figure is `distinct_collaborators` (a displayed-only stat counting ALL review interactions, not just substantive ones), while "50" is the substantive-review count with only 19 distinct qualifying reviewed authors. The text conflates two different metrics — fix the wording to not imply 65 relates to the 50 substantive reviews (e.g. separate the two facts clearly, or cite the 19-author figure alongside the 50-review count).
- Important process gap: the five why_overrides entries currently exist ONLY as a one-off patch made directly to data/scores.json with an inline Python command — scripts/score.py does not generate or preserve them at all, so rerunning score.py (required for fixes #1-#4) will silently delete them. Update the existing 5 entries' text per the two bullet points above while you're at it, and after re-scoring, regenerate/re-pick which 5 (or however many) top engineers need why_overrides entries — the top 5 may change once bugs #1-#4 are fixed, so make sure whoever ends up in the actual new top 5 has a why_overrides entry with accurate, verified text (each claim must be checkable against the actual PR/review data, not invented).

6	
7	## Approach
8	
9	"Impact" here is deliberately **not** LOC, commit count, or PR count — those measure activity, not impact, and are the explicit red flag this assignment calls out. Instead, every engineer gets a composite **Impact Score (0–100)**, computed only from **merged** PRs in the last 90 days (2026-06-17 to 2026-09-15), from three components:
10	
11	| Component | Weight | What it measures |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| **Shipped Scope / Blast Radius** | 45% | Structural reach — did this PR touch files many *other* engineers also depend on, vs. an isolated corner of the codebase? Computed via co-touch centrality across a file→authors map built from the whole window, not by counting directories or lines changed. |
14	| **Leverage on Others** | 35% | Substantive reviews given to teammates (non-trivial comment body, not rubber-stamp approvals), multiplied by `log1p` of the number of distinct people reviewed. No speed proxy is used. |
15	| **Domain Stewardship** | 20% | Sustained authored + reviewed activity in a subsystem — derived by parsing each PR's conventional-commit scope (`feat(scope): …`), falling back to the dominant top-level file path when a title has no scope, then crediting the top-2 most active engineers per scope. |
16	
17	All three are **percentile-ranked** (not min-max normalized) across the eligible engineer set, so a single high-volume outlier can't compress everyone else's score. There is **no minimum-activity eligibility floor** — someone who shipped one large piece of infrastructure and spent the rest of the window reviewing can still surface at the top.
18	
19	Bot accounts (including GitHub App actors such as StampHog, CodeRabbit, Greptile, and Graphite) and mechanical PRs (lockfile-only diffs and dependency bumps) are excluded from scoring. Volume stays visible without driving the ranking.
20	
21	**Ranking is fully deterministic** (Python, `scripts/score.py`) — no LLM anywhere in the scoring path, so there's no risk of a drifting classifier silently distorting the number. The only place AI touches the output is writing the one-clause "why" text for the top 5 cards' supporting PR evidence, applied *after* ranking is settled.
22	
23	Every card links directly to 2–3 real PRs on GitHub, so a reviewer can validate the ranking by clicking through rather than trusting a bare number.
24	
25	### Data
26	
27	- Source: `gh api graphql` against `PostHog/posthog`, sliced by single calendar day (GitHub's search API caps at 1000 results per query, and this repo merges ~150–250 PRs/day — a single 90-day query would have silently truncated).
28	- Fetched count is checked against GitHub's own reported count for every day slice (see `data/raw_prs.json` → `meta.per_day_mismatches`).
29	- Nested review and file connections are cursor-paginated to completion. The checked-in legacy snapshot was initially fetched at 20 files and 10 reviews per PR; `data/review_completions.json` recovers every review connection that hit that cap, while the fetcher now completes both connection types on future full refreshes. Until that full shell refresh can run, file co-touch for legacy PRs above 20 files remains a truncated sample and may understate or overstate their structural reach.
30	- Raw data and the scoring script are committed to this repo (`data/raw_prs.json`, `data/scores.json`, `scripts/`) so the analysis is reproducible, not just decorative.
31	
32	### Stack
33	
34	Local snapshot → Python scoring → static JSON → static HTML → GitHub Pages. No backend, no database, no live GitHub calls at view time — the dashboard loads a pre-computed `data/scores.json` alongside `index.html`, which keeps load time well under the 10s bar and means the page works even if GitHub's API is unavailable when a reviewer opens it.

input.content:
← PostHog Engineering Impact

Roadmap

What's next

The dashboard scores individuals over one fixed 90-day window because that was the right scope for a time-boxed build. Two things came up while building it that a real engineering leader would actually want next — both listed first, both genuinely bigger than a 90-minute add-on. The rest is a shorter list of smaller, deferred ideas.

The two big ones

Next

Subsystem / module drill-down

Right now Domain Stewardship is a single number folded into each engineer's score — it doesn't say which subsystems, or who else is active there. A dedicated per-scope view (billing, flags, ai-research, plugin-server, …) would show, for one subsystem at a time:

  • Everyone active there this window, ranked — not just the top-2 who earn scoring credit
  • Subsystem-level context: PR volume, review latency, bot-vs-human PR mix
  • A bus-factor flag — subsystems where stewardship credit concentrates in a single person are a single-point-of-failure risk, and that's arguably the single most actionable thing a subsystem view could surface. It's a more useful question for a leader than "who's #1 overall": "which parts of the codebase have exactly one person who really knows them?"

Mechanically cheap to add — the scope is already parsed and stored per PR (see the stewardship methodology) — the work is mainly a new aggregation pass and a second page template, not a new data pipeline.

Next

Trends over time

The current dashboard is one static snapshot of a single 90-day window. That can't distinguish "consistently strong contributor" from "caught a temporary spike right before the window closed" — and it gives no sense of whether the whole org's pace this quarter was normal or unusual. A time-series view would add:

  • Rolling per-engineer Impact Score over several trailing windows (e.g. weekly, each still a 90-day lookback) — a trajectory, not a point estimate
  • Org-wide series: merged PR volume, review latency, bot-vs-human PR mix, week over week — the context a single snapshot can't provide
  • Ramp-up tracking for newly active engineers — e.g. time to first substantive review given, as an onboarding-health signal distinct from the impact score itself

The scoring logic (scripts/score.py) is already parameterized by a date window, so this is largely a re-run-at-multiple-windows problem rather than a redesign — the real cost is the data footprint (multiple 90-day fetches instead of one) and the GraphQL rate-limit budget that comes with it, which is why it didn't fit the original time box.

Smaller deferred ideas

Later

Team rollups

If GitHub Teams or a CODEOWNERS-style mapping were incorporated, scores could roll up to team level, not just individual — useful for a leader who thinks in terms of teams first and people second.

Later

Cross-repo scope

Currently scoped to posthog/posthog only. PostHog engineers also ship to posthog-js and other repos in the org — a fuller picture would pull from all of them, deduplicated by author across repos.

Later

Tenure-aware normalization

A two-month-old hire and a three-year veteran are being percentile-ranked against the same pool right now. Normalizing by tenure (or at least segmenting new joiners into their own comparison group for their first quarter) would make the score fairer without diluting the "who's the best right now" read for everyone else.

Later

Reliability signal

PR titles containing "revert," or issues explicitly closed by a PR (GraphQL's closingIssuesReferences, a field not currently fetched), could support a light reliability/impact-on-users signal — shipped work that measurably fixed something reported, versus work that had to be walked back. Deliberately not folded into the score without more validation that it wouldn't just penalize people who ship more (and therefore revert more, in absolute terms).

Later

Real avatars, scheduled regeneration

Two smaller polish items: pull each engineer's actual GitHub avatar instead of a bare login string, and move from a one-off manual snapshot to a scheduled GitHub Actions job that regenerates data/scores.json on a cadence (nightly or weekly) so the dashboard stays current without a person re-running the pipeline by hand.

Deliberately never

An LLM will not be added to the ranking path. This is a design decision, not a gap to fill later — see the methodology overview for why ranking stays fully deterministic. AI-assisted text generation (the "why" card copy) stays scoped to summarizing evidence after a ranking is already fixed by plain arithmetic, and that boundary is intentional going forward too.
← Back to the dashboard · Methodology

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	Fetch all merged PRs for PostHog/posthog in the last 90 days via GraphQL,
4	sliced by single calendar day to stay safely under GitHub search's
5	1000-result-per-query cap. The initial query fetches 100 files and 10 reviews
6	per PR, then cursor-paginates every truncated nested connection. This keeps
7	individual query cost predictable without silently dropping evidence.
8	"""
9	import json
10	import subprocess
11	import sys
12	import time
13	from datetime import date, timedelta
14	
15	REPO = "PostHog/posthog"
16	START = date(2026, 6, 17)
17	END = date(2026, 9, 15)
18	OUT_PATH = "data/raw_prs.json"
19	
20	QUERY = """
21	query($cursor: String) {
22	  rateLimit { cost remaining resetAt }
23	  search(query: "repo:%s is:pr is:merged merged:%s..%s", type: ISSUE, first: 50, after: $cursor) {
24	    issueCount
25	    pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }
26	    nodes {
27	      ... on PullRequest {
28	        id
29	        number
30	        title
31	        url
32	        mergedAt
33	        createdAt
34	        changedFiles
35	        author { login __typename }
36	        files(first: 100) {
37	          totalCount
38	          pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }
39	          nodes { path }
40	        }
41	        reviews(first: 10) {
42	          totalCount
43	          pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }
44	          nodes { author { login __typename } state body submittedAt }
45	        }
46	        labels(first: 5) { nodes { name } }
47	      }
48	    }
49	  }
50	}
51	"""
52	
53	
54	def gh_graphql(query_text, cursor=None, retries=5):
55	    for attempt in range(retries):
56	        args = ["gh", "api", "graphql", "-f", f"query={query_text}"]
57	        if cursor:
58	            args += ["-f", f"cursor={cursor}"]
59	        result = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True)
60	        if result.returncode == 0:
61	            return json.loads(result.stdout)
62	        sys.stderr.write(f"  retry {attempt+1}: {result.stderr[:300]}\n")
63	        time.sleep(2 * (attempt + 1))
64	    raise RuntimeError(f"gh api graphql failed after {retries} retries")
65	
66	
67	def paginate_nested(prs, field, node_selection, page_size, batch_size=40):
68	    """Complete a nested PR connection in cost-bounded alias batches."""
69	    pending = [
70	        (pr, pr[field]["pageInfo"]["endCursor"])
71	        for pr in prs
72	        if pr[field]["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]
73	    ]
74	    pages = 0
75	    while pending:
76	        batch, pending = pending[:batch_size], pending[batch_size:]
77	        aliases = []
78	        for i, (pr, cursor) in enumerate(batch):
79	            aliases.append(
80	                f'r{i}: node(id: {json.dumps(pr["id"])}) {{ '
81	                f'... on PullRequest {{ {field}(first: {page_size}, after: {json.dumps(cursor)}) {{ '
82	                f'totalCount pageInfo {{ hasNextPage endCursor }} nodes {{ {node_selection} }} '
83	                f'}} }} }}'
84	            )
85	        query = "query { rateLimit { cost remaining resetAt } " + " ".join(aliases) + " }"
86	        data = gh_graphql(query)["data"]
87	        remaining = data["rateLimit"]["remaining"]
88	        for i, (pr, _) in enumerate(batch):
89	            page = data[f"r{i}"][field]
90	            pr[field]["nodes"].extend(page["nodes"])
91	            pr[field]["totalCount"] = page["totalCount"]
92	            pr[field]["pageInfo"] = page["pageInfo"]
93	            pages += 1
94	            if page["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]:
95	                pending.append((pr, page["pageInfo"]["endCursor"]))
96	        print(
97	            f"  completed {field}: pages={pages} pending={len(pending)} "
98	            f"rate_remaining={remaining}",
99	            flush=True,
100	        )
101	        if remaining < 200:
102	            sys.stderr.write(f"  rate limit low ({remaining}), pausing 60s\n")
103	            time.sleep(60)
104	    return pages
105	
106	
107	def fetch_day(day_str):
108	    prs = []
109	    cursor = None
110	    total_reported = None
111	    while True:
112	        q = QUERY % (REPO, day_str, day_str)
113	        data = gh_graphql(q, cursor)
114	        remaining = data["data"]["rateLimit"]["remaining"]
115	        search = data["data"]["search"]
116	        total_reported = search["issueCount"]
117	        prs.extend(search["nodes"])
118	        if not search["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]:
119	            break
120	        cursor = search["pageInfo"]["endCursor"]
121	        if remaining < 200:
122	            sys.stderr.write(f"  rate limit low ({remaining}), pausing 60s\n")
123	            time.sleep(60)
124	    return prs, total_reported, remaining
125	
126	
127	def main():
128	    all_prs = {}
129	    day = START
130	    mismatches = []
131	    day_count = 0
132	    total_days = (END - START).days + 1
133	    while day <= END:
134	        day_str = day.isoformat()
135	        prs, reported, remaining = fetch_day(day_str)
136	        fetched = len(prs)
137	        if fetched != reported:
138	            mismatches.append({"day": day_str, "reported": reported, "fetched": fetched})
139	        for pr in prs:
140	            all_prs[pr["number"]] = pr
141	        day_count += 1
142	        print(f"[{day_count}/{total_days}] {day_str}: reported={reported} fetched={fetched} "
143	              f"running_total={len(all_prs)} rate_remaining={remaining}", flush=True)
144	        day = day + timedelta(days=1)
145	
146	    all_prs_list = list(all_prs.values())
147	    review_pages = paginate_nested(
148	        all_prs_list,
149	        "reviews",
150	        "author { login __typename } state body submittedAt",
151	        100,
152	    )
153	    file_pages = paginate_nested(all_prs_list, "files", "path", 100)
154	
155	    incomplete_reviews = sum(
156	        len(pr["reviews"]["nodes"]) != pr["reviews"]["totalCount"]
157	        for pr in all_prs_list
158	    )
159	    incomplete_files = sum(
160	        len(pr["files"]["nodes"]) != pr["files"]["totalCount"]
161	        for pr in all_prs_list
162	    )
163	    if incomplete_reviews or incomplete_files:
164	        raise RuntimeError(
165	            f"nested pagination incomplete: reviews={incomplete_reviews}, files={incomplete_files}"
166	        )
167	
168	    with open(OUT_PATH, "w") as f:
169	        json.dump({
170	            "meta": {
171	                "repo": REPO,
172	                "window_start": START.isoformat(),
173	                "window_end": END.isoformat(),
174	                "total_prs": len(all_prs),
175	                "per_day_mismatches": mismatches,
176	                "initial_page_sizes": {"files_per_pr": 100, "reviews_per_pr": 10},
177	                "nested_pagination": {
178	                    "review_pages_fetched": review_pages,
179	                    "file_pages_fetched": file_pages,
180	                    "incomplete_review_connections": incomplete_reviews,
181	                    "incomplete_file_connections": incomplete_files,
182	                },
183	            },
184	            "prs": all_prs_list,
185	        }, f)
186	
187	    print(f"\nDone. {len(all_prs)} unique merged PRs written to {OUT_PATH}")
188	    if mismatches:
189	        print(f"WARNING: {len(mismatches)} day(s) had reported != fetched count:")
190	        for m in mismatches:
191	            print(f"  {m}")
192	
193	
194	if __name__ == "__main__":
195	    main()
196

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	Deterministic scoring: no LLM anywhere in this file. Reads data/raw_prs.json,
4	computes the three weighted components (Shipped Scope 45%, Leverage on Others 35%,
5	Domain Stewardship 20%), rank-normalizes each, and writes data/scores.json.
6	"""
7	import json
8	import math
9	import re
10	from collections import Counter, defaultdict
11	
12	IN_PATH = "data/raw_prs.json"
13	OUT_PATH = "data/scores.json"
14	WHY_OVERRIDES_PATH = "data/why_overrides.json"
15	REVIEW_COMPLETIONS_PATH = "data/review_completions.json"
16	
17	BOT_MARKERS = [
18	    "[bot]", "dependabot", "renovate", "coderabbitai", "greptile",
19	    "sourcery", "copilot", "codecov", "snyk", "semgrep", "github-actions",
20	    "stamphog", "graphite-app", "posthog-security-review-bot",
21	    "exe-dev-github-integration",
22	]
23	LOCKFILES = {
24	    "package-lock.json", "yarn.lock", "pnpm-lock.yaml", "poetry.lock",
25	    "Cargo.lock", "Gemfile.lock", "uv.lock",
26	}
27	SCOPE_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z]+\(([^)]+)\):")
28	
29	
30	def is_bot(login, typename):
31	    if typename == "Bot":
32	        return True
33	    l = (login or "").lower()
34	    if l.endswith("bot"):
35	        return True
36	    return any(m in l for m in BOT_MARKERS)
37	
38	
39	def is_mechanical(title, files):
40	    t = title.lower()
41	    if "chore(deps)" in t or t.startswith("bump ") or " bump " in t:
42	        return True
43	    if files and all(f.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] in LOCKFILES for f in files):
44	        return True
45	    return False
46	
47	
48	def parse_scope(title, files):
49	    m = SCOPE_RE.match(title.strip())
50	    if m:
51	        return m.group(1), False
52	    segs = [f.split("/")[0] for f in files if f]
53	    if not segs:
54	        return "unknown", True
55	    return Counter(segs).most_common(1)[0][0], True
56	
57	
58	def rank_normalize(values):
59	    """Percentile rank 0-100, ties averaged. values: dict[key] -> float."""
60	    items = sorted(values.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
61	    n = len(items)
62	    if n == 0:
63	        return {}
64	    if n == 1:
65	        return {items[0][0]: 0.0 if items[0][1] == 0 else 100.0}
66	    result = {}
67	    i = 0
68	    while i < n:
69	        j = i
70	        while j + 1 < n and items[j + 1][1] == items[i][1]:
71	            j += 1
72	        avg_rank = (i + j) / 2
73	        pct = 0.0 if items[i][1] == 0 else avg_rank / (n - 1) * 100
74	        for k in range(i, j + 1):
75	            result[items[k][0]] = pct
76	        i = j + 1
77	    return result
78	
79	
80	def main():
81	    with open(IN_PATH) as f:
82	        raw = json.load(f)
83	    prs = raw["prs"]
84	    meta = raw["meta"]
85	    try:
86	        with open(REVIEW_COMPLETIONS_PATH) as f:
87	            review_completions_doc = json.load(f)
88	            review_completions = review_completions_doc["reviews"]
89	    except FileNotFoundError:
90	        review_completions_doc = {"meta": {}}
91	        review_completions = {}

# PostHog Engineering Impact Dashboard

Weave take-home: identify the most impactful engineers on `posthog/posthog` over the last 90 days.

**Live dashboard:** https://jeromebanks.github.io/posthog-impact-dashboard/

## Approach

"Impact" here is deliberately **not** LOC, commit count, or PR count — those measure activity, not impact, and are the explicit red flag this assignment calls out. Instead, every engineer gets a composite **Impact Score (0–100)**, computed only from **merged** PRs in the last 90 days (2026-06-17 to 2026-09-15), from three components:

| Component | Weight | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Shipped Scope / Blast Radius** | 45% | Structural reach — did this PR touch files many *other* engineers also depend on, vs. an isolated corner of the codebase? Computed via co-touch centrality across a file→authors map built from the whole window, not by counting directories or lines changed. |
| **Leverage on Others** | 35% | Substantive reviews given to teammates (non-trivial comment body, not rubber-stamp approvals), multiplied by `log1p` of the number of distinct people reviewed. No speed proxy is used. |
| **Domain Stewardship** | 20% | Sustained authored + reviewed activity in a subsystem — derived by parsing each PR's conventional-commit scope (`feat(scope): …`), falling back to the dominant top-level file path when a title has no scope, then crediting the top-2 most active engineers per scope. |

All three are **percentile-ranked** (not min-max normalized) across the eligible engineer set, so a single high-volume outlier can't compress everyone else's score. There is **no minimum-activity eligibility floor** — someone who shipped one large piece of infrastructure and spent the rest of the window reviewing can still surface at the top.

Bot accounts (including GitHub App actors such as StampHog, CodeRabbit, Greptile, and Graphite) and mechanical PRs (lockfile-only diffs and dependency bumps) are excluded from scoring. Volume stays visible without driving the ranking.

**Ranking is fully deterministic** (Python, `scripts/score.py`) — no LLM anywhere in the scoring path, so there's no risk of a drifting classifier silently distorting the number. The only place AI touches the output is writing the one-clause "why" text for the top 5 cards' supporting PR evidence, applied *after* ranking is settled.

Every card links directly to 2–3 real PRs on GitHub, so a reviewer can validate the ranking by clicking through rather than trusting a bare number.

### Data

- Source: `gh api graphql` against `PostHog/posthog`, sliced by single calendar day (GitHub's search API caps at 1000 results per query, and this repo merges ~150–250 PRs/day — a single 90-day query would have silently truncated).
- Fetched count is checked against GitHub's own reported count for every day slice (see `data/raw_prs.json` → `meta.per_day_mismatches`).
- Nested review and file connections are cursor-paginated to completion. The checked-in legacy snapshot was initially fetched at 20 files and 10 reviews per PR; `data/review_completions.json` recovers every review connection that hit that cap, while the fetcher now completes both connection types on future full refreshes. Until that full shell refresh can run, file co-touch for legacy PRs above 20 files remains a truncated sample and may understate or overstate their structural reach.
- Raw data and the scoring script are committed to this repo (`data/raw_prs.json`, `data/scores.json`, `scripts/`) so the analysis is reproducible, not just decorative.

### Stack

Local snapshot → Python scoring → static JSON → static HTML → GitHub Pages. No backend, no database, no live GitHub calls at view time — the dashboard loads a pre-computed `data/scores.json` alongside `index.html`, which keeps load time well under the 10s bar and means the page works even if GitHub's API is unavailable when a reviewer opens it.

## Time

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Timeout → killed. Set `persistent: true` for session-length watches (PR monitoring, log tails) — the monitor runs until you call TaskStop or the session ends. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, max 3600000ms. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout). Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring or log tails. Stop with TaskStop.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# PostHog Engineering Impact Dashboard

Weave take-home: identify the most impactful engineers on `posthog/posthog` over the last 90 days.

**Live dashboard:** https://jeromebanks.github.io/posthog-impact-dashboard/

## Approach

"Impact" here is deliberately **not** LOC, commit count, or PR count — those measure activity, not impact, and are the explicit red flag this assignment calls out. Instead, every engineer gets a composite **Impact Score (0–100)**, computed only from **merged** PRs in the last 90 days (2026-06-17 to 2026-09-15), from three components:

| Component | Weight | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Shipped Scope / Blast Radius** | 45% | Structural reach — did this PR touch files many *other* engineers also depend on, vs. an isolated corner of the codebase? Computed via co-touch centrality across a file→authors map built from the whole window, not by counting directories or lines changed. |
| **Leverage on Others** | 35% | Substantive reviews given to teammates (non-trivial comment body, not rubber-stamp approvals), multiplied by `log1p` of the number of distinct people reviewed. No speed proxy is used. |
| **Domain Stewardship** | 20% | Sustained authored + reviewed activity in a subsystem — derived by parsing each PR's conventional-commit scope (`feat(scope): …`), falling back to the dominant top-level file path when a title has no scope, then crediting the top-2 most active engineers per scope. |

All three are **percentile-ranked** (not min-max normalized) across the eligible engineer set, so a single high-volume outlier can't compress everyone else's score. There is **no minimum-activity eligibility floor** — someone who shipped one large piece of infrastructure and spent the rest of the window reviewing can still surface at the top.

Bot accounts (including GitHub App actors such as StampHog, CodeRabbit, Greptile, and Graphite) and mechanical PRs (lockfile-only diffs and dependency bumps) are excluded from scoring. Volume stays visible without driving the ranking.

**Ranking is fully deterministic** (Python, `scripts/score.py`) — no LLM anywhere in the scoring path, so there's no risk of a drifting classifier silently distorting the number. The only place AI touches the output is writing the one-clause "why" text for the top 5 cards' supporting PR evidence, applied *after* ranking is settled.

Every card links directly to 2–3 real PRs on GitHub, so a reviewer can validate the ranking by clicking through rather than trusting a bare number.

### Data

- Source: `gh api graphql` against `PostHog/posthog`, sliced by single calendar day (GitHub's search API caps at 1000 results per query, and this repo merges ~150–250 PRs/day — a single 90-day query would have silently truncated).
- Fetched count is checked against GitHub's own reported count for every day slice (see `data/raw_prs.json` → `meta.per_day_mismatches`).
- Nested review and file connections are cursor-paginated to completion. The checked-in legacy snapshot was initially fetched at 20 files and 10 reviews per PR; `data/review_completions.json` recovers every review connection that hit that cap, while the fetcher now completes both connection types on future full refreshes. Until that full shell refresh can run, file co-touch for legacy PRs above 20 files remains a truncated sample and may understate or overstate their structural reach.
- Raw data and the scoring script are committed to this repo (`data/raw_prs.json`, `data/scores.json`, `scripts/`) so the analysis is reproducible, not just decorative.

### Stack

Local snapshot → Python scoring → static JSON → static HTML → GitHub Pages. No backend, no database, no live GitHub calls at view time — the dashboard loads a pre-computed `data/scores.json` alongside `index.html`, which keeps load time well under the 10s bar and means the page works even if GitHub's API is unavailable when a reviewer opens it.

## Time

| **Shipped Scope / Blast Radius** | 45% | Structural reach — did this PR touch files many *other* engineers also depend on, vs. an isolated corner of the codebase? Computed via co-touch centrality across a file→authors map built from the whole window, not by counting directories or lines changed. |
| **Leverage on Others** | 35% | Substantive reviews given to teammates (non-trivial comment body, not rubber-stamp approvals), multiplied by `log1p` of the number of distinct people reviewed. No speed proxy is used. |
| **Domain Stewardship** | 20% | Sustained authored + reviewed activity in a subsystem — derived by parsing each PR's conventional-commit scope (`feat(scope): …`), falling back to the dominant top-level file path when a title has no scope, then crediting the top-2 most active engineers per scope. |

All three are **percentile-ranked** (not min-max normalized) across the eligible engineer set, so a single high-volume outlier can't compress everyone else's score. There is **no minimum-activity eligibility floor** — someone who shipped one large piece of infrastructure and spent the rest of the window reviewing can still surface at the top.

Bot accounts (including GitHub App actors such as StampHog, CodeRabbit, Greptile, and Graphite) and mechanical PRs (lockfile-only diffs and dependency bumps) are excluded from scoring. Volume stays visible without driving the ranking.

**Ranking is fully deterministic** (Python, `scripts/score.py`) — no LLM anywhere in the scoring path, so there's no risk of a drifting classifier silently distorting the number. The only place AI touches the output is writing the one-clause "why" text for the top 5 cards' supporting PR evidence, applied *after* ranking is settled.

Every card links directly to 2–3 real PRs on GitHub, so a reviewer can validate the ranking by clicking through rather than trusting a bare number.

### Data

- Source: `gh api graphql` against `PostHog/posthog`, sliced by single calendar day (GitHub's search API caps at 1000 results per query, and this repo merges ~150–290 PRs/day — a single 90-day query would have silently truncated).
- Fetched count is checked against GitHub's own reported count for every day slice (0 mismatches across all 91 days — see `data/raw_prs.json` → `meta.per_day_mismatches`).
- **Known, disclosed limitation**: each PR's initial fetch caps at 20 files and 10 reviews. `scripts/fetch_prs.py` was later rewritten to cursor-paginate both connections to completion, but a fresh full re-fetch (91 day-slices plus a batched pagination-completion pass) didn't fit in the remaining time and was stopped partway through rather than ship a rushed, partially-verified dataset. **1,737 of 15,078 PRs (11.5%) have exactly 10 fetched reviews** and may have additional reviews beyond that cap (automated tools like CodeRabbit/Greptile could occupy some of those 10 slots ahead of human reviews on a given PR); **1,555 (10.3%) have exactly 20 files** and may understate that PR's true co-touch weight in Shipped Scope. This is disclosed rather than silently absorbed into the ranking — see the [roadmap](roadmap.html) for the fix (the code for it already exists in `fetch_prs.py`, it just wasn't run to completion).
- Bot-authored PRs and known automated reviewers (Dependabot, Renovate, CodeRabbit, Greptile, and PostHog's own internal review bot `stamphog`, discovered mid-build with 7,454 review mentions — see commit history) are excluded from scoring by account type and a login-pattern backstop.
- Raw data and the scoring script are committed to this repo (`data/raw_prs.json`, `data/scores.json`, `scripts/`) so the analysis is reproducible, not just decorative.

### Stack

Local snapshot → Python scoring → static JSON → static HTML → GitHub Pages. No backend, no database, no live GitHub calls at view time — the dashboard loads a pre-computed `data/scores.json` alongside `index.html`, which keeps load time well under the 10s bar and means the page works even if GitHub's API is unavailable when a reviewer opens it.
